newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr squeezes higher as rates held steady.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr squeezes higher as rates held steady.

text.p: The Australian dollar posted its strongest close for the week as the local market covered short positions established in case the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) had decided to ease interest rates on Friday.
The RBA remained silent at its morning announcement time, and now the market does not see a realistic easing opportunity for another two weeks.
By 5.00 p.m. (0700 GMT), the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7445/50, up from an early US$0.7416/21 and a close on Thursday of US$0.7425/30.

Despite the RBA not moving today, expectations that another cut is likely to occur will continue to cap the dollar, and also prevented a sizeable rally after no cut was announced. It did, however, remove some immediate pressure from the unit.
"Everyone was quite keen for an interest rate cut today, and once we didn't have the cut the Aussie didn't rally at all," one trader said, saying it gradually edged higher.
"Most players were short, and what we're finding this afternoon is the trading banks are just sick of being short today, and once it went over US$0.7435 they started covering."

There was also solid Aussie/yen buying, which saw it rise a full yen, ending at 84.67/77 yen from an early 83.83/93 and a Thursday close of 83.63/73. In trade weighted terms, it ended at 56.9, up on Thursday's 56.6 and its highest close in a week.

May housing finance data showing a slightly larger than expected 8.4 percent fall in approvals had little impact on the market, and was not as weak as it appeared as it followed a 12.2 percent rise the previous month.
Friday's rate cut expectations were built on Thursday's weaker than expected June labour force data, although a move on the back of bad news was always seen as an outside chance.

Instead, the RBA was seen waiting until after June quarter inflation and wages data is released on July 23 and 24. Until then, the ongoing expectations of a rate cut were expected to cap the dollar, with selling appearing on rallies.

On the downside, rumours of an Asian player protecting a large options position around US$0.7410 were provinding a solid floor, but traders felt that if the dollar was going to break its current rangee soon, it would be on the downside.
With no major data due next week, the local focus will be on the inflation and wages data, which economists surveyed by Reuters expect to be very bullish for an interest rate cut.
The consumer price index is expected to be flat in the quarter, and to have risen just 0.6 percent over the year.

The underlying rate of inflation, which the RBA targets, is expected to fall out of the bottom of the two to three percent target zone for the first time since March 1995. In fact, if the median forecast of a 1.7 percent annual rise is realised, it will be the lowest annual rate since the series began in the early 1970s.
Wages, a key determinant of underlying inflation, were seen coming in well under the RBA's 4.5 percent speed limit.
Combined with a weak labour market and excess capacity in many sectors of the economy, the odds favoured another rate cut, analysts said.
For the Australian dollar that meant that while a short covering rally, possibly to above US$0.7500, could occur, the pressure should remain to the downside, traders said.
